title: SLO-bound tenant scheduler and shiftable compute (PRD - rough)
content:
Status: rough PRD / proto design notes. Goal: capture a concrete design for per-tenant SLO-aware scheduling that supports (a) burst accommodation, (b) controlled compute shifting (model fidelity/region), and (c) tenant isolation constraints, with an operator-facing API and a simple simulator to validate tradeoffs.

Background / motivation:
- Customers on Dedicated want predictable 99th/95th latency SLAs while still retaining cost efficiency and the ability to absorb sudden bursts. Current approaches are either heavy-handed (static reservations) or overly optimistic (best-effort autoscalers). We need a middle ground: policy-driven scheduling that treats SLOs as first-class primitives and enables transient reconfiguration (shiftable compute) under bounded rules.

Problem statement:
- Provide a scheduling layer that:
  1) Guarantees latency envelopes for reserved requests (by tenant) under normal and mild surge conditions.
  2) Allows tenants to opt into controlled degradation modes (e.g., quantized model, regional reroute) in exchange for lower cost or burst credits.
  3) Enforces isolation so noisy tenants cannot systematically eat others' headroom.
  4) Offers clear operator tooling and metrics to reason about tradeoffs.

High-level concept: SLO Envelopes + Shiftable Compute
- SLO Envelope: each tenant declares (or is assigned) an SLO profile: {latency_target_ms, percentile, burst_window_sec, burst_budget_tokens}. The scheduler ensures compute/headroom allocations to meet the envelope.
- Shiftable Compute Policy: tenants may provide a policy allowing the platform to shift work along a small, policy-defined dimension set: model_fidelity (full/half/quantized), region_preference (primary/secondary), or compute_tier (dedicated/spot-burst). The policy includes allowed transitions, max-duration-per-transition, and penalty coefficients (e.g., expected quality delta).
- Burst Tokens: a temporal credit ledger per tenant (burst_budget_tokens) used to permit operations outside steady-state reservations. Tokens are earned at steady usage and can be purchased/allocated via commitment tiers.

Design components:
1) Admission controller (front-door): validates incoming requests against current envelope state. Rejects or routes to degraded paths if SLO would be violated.
2) Scheduler (servo loop): maintains a global view of active envelopes, current utilization, and pool health. Runs a lightweight optimization every 10s to:
   - Allocate/constrain request routing to compute pools.
   - Trigger shiftable compute transitions per tenant policy if helpful.
   - Move ephemeral prewarm slots between tenants if headroom > threshold.
3) Policy DB: tenant-level SLO profile and shiftable-compute permissions. Exposed via API.
4) Fallback graph: pre-defined compatible variants per model (e.g., llama-13b -> llama-13b-q4 -> llama-7b-8k) and region-compatible endpoints. The scheduler uses this graph to evaluate fallback chains.

APIs (operator + customer facing):
- PUT /tenants/{id}/slo-profile -> set latency_target_ms, percentile, burst_window_sec, burst_budget_tokens, isolation_class
- POST /tenants/{id}/shiftable-policy -> allowed_transitions, max_duration_s, quality_penalties, opt_in_flag
- GET /tenants/{id}/ledger -> current burst tokens, earned_rate, spent_history
- POST /simulation/run -> run a what-if simulation (internal) with traffic trace

Behavioral rules / constraints (proposal):
- SLO-first routing: route to primary pool if it will meet envelope; else, consult shiftable-policy and ledger. If tenant opts into model_fidelity transitions and has tokens, allowed to degrade.
- Isolation classes: hard (no cross-tenant prewarm), soft (can borrow ephemeral prewarm but subject to repayment), pooled (sharing allowed with capped share).
- Degradation safety: any transition that changes model_fidelity must not be longer than max_duration_s and must have a cool-down period to avoid oscillation.

Operator runbook (quick):
- Indicator: sustained 99th p99 > target -> check scheduler logs for which tenants hit envelope violations.
- If violations due to noisy neighbor: escalate to tenant isolation mode (move to hard isolation) and reprovision ephemeral prewarm.
- If global shortage: enable system-wide soft degrade with opt-in first tenants (low-cost tiers) and notify customers.

Simulator notes & preliminary results (toy sim):
- setup: 12 tenants, mixed SLOs: 4x (p99 200ms), 6x (p99 400ms), 2x (best-effort). Workload: base load + Poisson bursts (lambda=0.08 per tenant per min). Pools: 3 dedicated pools (A,B,C) with different cold-start profiles.
- policy: tenants with higher p99 had no degradation allowed; mid-tier tenants allowed model_fidelity degrade to q4 for up to 30s; burst tokens earned at 1 token/min, burst request costs 10 tokens.
- outcome: with SLO scheduler + shiftable compute we observed: average requested re-routes down 35%, overall infra footprint reduction ~12% (fewer prewarm slots), and p99 violations reduced 60% vs naive autoscale under same capacity budget. Cost reduction estimate: ~18% on token spend for mid-tier tenants due to opportunistic quantized inference during microbursts.
- caveats: toy sim assumptions optimistic on degraded-model quality and cold start overlap. Need more realistic traces.

UX / Console changes (operator + customer):
- New dashboard: Tenant SLO profiles, current envelope utilization, token ledger, active shift transitions, recent fallback events.
- Alerting: Tenant breach warnings (grace window) + global capacity pressure alerts.

Open questions / risks:
- Quality regression visibility: how to tie customer-visible quality metrics to allowed degradations? Need linkage to Redwood Optimize evals or prompt-set checks.
- Economic model: how do we price burst tokens and how do they interact with committed capacity billing?
- Legal / compliance: region-based reroute might violate data residency for some tenants — must honor per-tenant residency constraints.
- Oscillation risk: frequent shift oscillation could hurt cache effectiveness and increase tail latency; need guardrails (min_duration, cool-down, hysteresis).

Non-goals:
- Not attempting full multi-cluster allocation optimization in this phase.
- Not replacing existing Dedicated reservation UI; instead, augment it.

Implementation roadmap (MVP):
- Phase 0 (2w): API + policy DB + small admission validator (no scheduler changes) to allow storing SLO profiles and shift policies.
- Phase 1 (6w): Lightweight scheduler loop, simple fallback graph, per-tenant token ledger, and console visualizations. Internal-only rollout and E2E sim.
- Phase 2 (8w): Integration with routing layer, operator runbooks, opt-in tenant pilots, and billing hooks for token purchases.

Success metrics (rolling 90d):
- Reduction in p99 violations for opt-in tenants by >=50% versus baseline.
- Cost per served token for opt-in tenants reduced >=10% (after accounting for token purchases).
- No data residency violations (0 incidents).

Next steps / immediate TODOs:
- Run 3 more sims with latency traces from infra (ask SRE for traces). (ACTION: @Marcus Liu)
- Draft a short customer-facing one-pager to offer as pilot program. (ACTION: @Ava Patel)
- Create a Linear epic and include API sketches and alerting wireframes.

Notes to self / scribbles:
- Could combine with predictive warm-pool signals later (if we can cheaply predict burst start).
- Consider a gradual tradeoff curve rather than binary degrade (multi-step fidelity ladder).
- Think about per-tenant QoE cameras (sample generations) to automatically detect unacceptable quality drops.

References / pointers:
- See: github PR for simple fallback-graph prototype: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/196
- Related: linear DED-412 (scheduler proto)
